profile.campus: Fort Worth, Tarrant County, Texas (QTS Fort Worth / FTW1 campus, one of QTS's two Dallas-area mega-scale campuses)
profile.address: 14100 Park Vista Boulevard, Fort Worth, TX 76177
profile.reading:
Per QTS's own facility page, FTW1 DC1 sits at 14100 Park Vista Boulevard, Fort Worth, TX 76177, part of a 52-acre campus (with 12 adjacent acres reserved for future expansion) alongside sibling building FTW1 DC2 (14052 Park Vista Blvd); the campus publishes 70+ MW of critical capacity currently, with 200 MW gross campus potential planned, an on-site substation with expansion capability, LEED certification, and leasable customer office/flex workspace. QTS describes Fort Worth as one of its two mega-scale Dallas-area campuses (the other being Irving, tracked elsewhere in this registry).

QTS was founded in 2003 in Overland Park, Kansas, and was taken private in a roughly $10 billion Blackstone Real Estate Income Trust (BREIT)-led acquisition completed August 31, 2021, per Blackstone's own press release; QTS is no longer an independent SEC filer.

QTS positions itself as a "hyperscale-neutral" wholesale and colocation landlord, leasing built data center capacity to enterprise, cloud, and hyperscale tenants rather than operating its own end-user cloud service, a business model it shares with peers such as Digital Realty and CyrusOne. Since Blackstone completed its roughly $10 billion take-private acquisition in August 2021, QTS has continued expanding across multiple US metros rather than slowing development, including major campus filings and expansions in Phoenix (a 750MW, 375-acre Glendale campus acquired for $255.3 million in July 2022) and Dallas-Fort Worth (its two mega-scale Irving and Fort Worth campuses), consistent with the scale of buildout QTS has also pursued in Northern Virginia, Georgia, and Ohio, tracked elsewhere in this registry.

QTS was originally founded in 2003 in Overland Park, Kansas by Chad Williams, and grew through a mix of acquisitions and ground-up construction into a national wholesale/colocation platform before its 2013 IPO as a publicly traded REIT; that public period ended with the 2021 Blackstone take-private deal. QTS's current published portfolio language describes over 30 facilities across North America and Europe on its own site, while Wikipedia gives a somewhat different approximate figure of 28 locations across 16 US states plus two Netherlands sites (Eemshaven and Groningen), a discrepancy this registry notes rather than resolves in favor of either source.

reading.body:
This QTS campus in Fort Worth operates 70 MW of critical capacity today across two buildings, with a planned expansion to 200 MW gross. Assuming 40 kW per rack as a common AI training density, the current 70 MW of IT load represents roughly 1,750 racks, and the planned 200 MW would serve approximately 5,000 racks. The campus is one of the largest published facilities in Texas by capacity, though its rank of 19th statewide reflects that Texas has 18 other published data center campuses and 133 mapped facilities overall.

The operator is Quality Technology Services, acquired by Blackstone in August 2021 and taken private. No certifications, grid interconnection details, or current tenant mix are published in the operator's specifications. The facility's two-building configuration and planned tripling of capacity suggest an active expansion agenda, though the timeline and power supply constraints for reaching 200 MW are not disclosed.

For AI workload evaluation, the decisive unknown is whether this campus can secure the grid power needed for its stated expansion. Texas published data center capacity stands at 468 MW across 18 facilities with public specs. If this QTS campus reaches its 200 MW plan, it would represent 43 percent of that published statewide total. Whether the local grid, interconnection queue, and water availability support that expansion is not indicated in the published specifications.
